content.p: In the first days after Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, the Soviet secret police killed thousands of prisoners held in their jails across the newly occupied western borderlands. The killings took place in western Ukraine, in prisons in Belarus and in the Baltic states, and they happened in a matter of days. Local people later called them the 1941 NKVD prison massacres. The dead were often found as the German army advanced. Understanding Society compares their scale and ferocity to the NKVD killing of Polish prisoners of war and members of the Polish elite at Katyn Forest in April 1940.

No single total is accepted by everyone. The National WWII Museum says historians estimate that between 10,000 and 40,000 people were killed in western Ukraine over about eight days, and that exact numbers cannot be known because reliable records are scarce. The Euromaidan Press, citing the Electronic Archive of the Ukrainian liberation movement, puts the figure for western Ukraine in June and July at 24 thousand. What follows sets out what the surviving records show, and where they disagree.
content.h2: Prisons full on the eve of war
content.p: The prisons were already crowded before the war began. Between February and June 1940 the Soviet authorities had arrested, imprisoned, deported or executed hundreds of thousands of people in the western territories they had taken in 1939. The National WWII Museum says those arrested in the western regions included anti-communists, former Polish officials, civil servants, army officers and Ukrainian nationalists. From April 1940 the arrests widened to relatives of people already convicted and to doctors, engineers, lawyers, journalists, university teachers, merchants and prosperous farmers. Those who had not been deported or sentenced to death were still in NKVD cells when the invasion came.

The museum estimates that close to 140,000 political prisoners were held in Soviet-run jails on the eve of the German attack. When the invasion began, the NKVD received evacuation order No. 00803, which the museum describes as an order to evacuate and liquidate political prisoners. Understanding Society, quoting the editors of a 2017 sourcebook, Ksenya Kiebuzinski and Alexander Motyl, says the killings were not a spontaneous act by a retreating army but were coordinated by Soviet authorities, and that many prisoners showed signs of torture before they were killed.
content.h2: The first days in western Ukraine
content.p: The National WWII Museum dates the start of the executions in western Ukraine to the morning of 23 June 1941. Prisoners were killed whether they had been sentenced for serious offences or were still waiting to be questioned. Methods differed from prison to prison. Some prisoners were shot in the back of the neck, and others were burned alive in locked cells. In Dubno, the museum says, inmates were shot and stabbed while they slept.

Lutsk is one of the cases the museum describes in most detail. The museum says prisoners were crowded into small cells under the pretence of a large evacuation. NKVD officers then called them by name into the courtyard, lined them up and threw grenades at the group while tanks fired machine guns. A few survivors were made to dig graves and bury the dead until their guards fled ahead of a German unit. Casualty estimates for Lutsk range from 1,500 to 4,000.

The museum also gives figures for other towns. It says that on 26 June the NKVD blew up two large cells holding about 1,200 women in Sambir, and that in Ivano-Frankivsk three basement cells were found stacked with close to 2,500 bodies. It puts the toll at between 800 and 1,500 in each of several other towns, including Zolochiv, Dobromyl, Chortkiv and Rivne. These are the National WWII Museum's figures; the other pages opened here do not confirm them town by town.
content.h2: Lviv and the Lontsky Street prison
content.p: Lviv is the case with the most documents among the pages opened here. The Kyiv Post, reporting on the museum in the former Lontsky Street prison, quotes Soviet archive documents showing that 1,366 of the prison's 3,638 detainees were executed between 22 and 28 June 1941. The museum itself says the number is closer to 1,700. The Kyiv Post also reports that 42 percent of the prisoners killed in Lviv in those last days came from this one prison.

The historian John-Paul Himka, quoted in the Understanding Society article, describes the Lviv killings across three prisons: Zamarstyniv Street, Brygidki and Lontsky Street. The museum posters he cites give 1,681 dead at Lontsky Street, 971 at Zamarstyniv Street and 739 at Brygidki. Himka argues that the Soviet authorities murdered the political prisoners because they could not evacuate them fast enough after the German attack. He also criticises the Lontsky Street museum for presenting only one side of events.

The Kyiv Post also quotes an account by a medical student, Ivan Kindrat, who went to the prison in the last days of June and later wrote that a large room off the courtyard was filled from top to bottom with corpses. The Kyiv Post also reports that the Germans filmed the scene soon after they reached Lviv and used the footage for propaganda. The EHRI portal, which holds the film record, describes scenes of exhumation at Brygidki and of Jews being beaten during what it calls the "prison action" of the Lviv pogrom of 1941. Its notes quote Himka saying that the building in the first scene should be identifiable from the prison's burn marks. The same notes say that the scholar Bernd Boll does not think a field of soldiers' corpses in the reel relates to Lviv.
content.h2: Lithuania: Telšiai and the Rainiai forest
content.p: The killings also reached Lithuania. A Lithuanian heritage site says that on 22 June 1941 Telšiai prison held 162 prisoners, 76 of them held for interrogation by the NKGB. On 24 June, as a Red Army unit surrounded the prison, a three-judge court was formed in a hurry and sentenced all 76 political prisoners to death. The other prisoners were released. The site says the condemned were loaded into trucks at dawn on 25 June and driven towards Luokė, to the Rainiai forest.

The site names Petras Raslanas, head of the NKGB in Telšiai county, as the organiser of the killings, and quotes his 1942 explanation that he was convinced there was "not a single innocent person there". It also quotes Domas Rocius, a participant, who said the shooting was carried out by Red Army men, and that Raslanas, an operational officer and a prison guard were among those present. The site says that when pits were opened on 28 June, most victims bore signs of torture, and that many could not be identified. It says that only 10 prisoners had been shot outright, and that the rest had died of torture or bayonet wounds. The site's story page gives 73 prisoners and the night of 24 to 25 June, but its chapel section gives 75 and 25 to 26 June. The site's memorial page gives 75 for the night of 24 to 25 June.

A chapel was built at Rainiai in 1943 to a design by Jonas Virakas. The Soviet authorities demolished it in 1944. After Lithuania regained independence, a new chapel was consecrated on 23 June 1991, the fiftieth anniversary of the killings. A memorial plaque at the former prison was unveiled in 1997.

In Riga, the Occupation Museum of Latvia says 99 men were shot without trial between 27 and 29 June 1941 in Riga Central Prison and buried in its courtyard. News of the killings reached the city on 1 July, when the German army entered Riga. The museum says two patches of freshly dug earth were found in the prison yard, and that exhumation yielded 98 bodies, with one more found separately. 69 were identified very soon, and the museum says no further identifications were made or information obtained.

The museum's historian Inese Dreimane spent two years on research that identified all 99 victims. The museum gives their nationalities as 79 Latvians, seven Russians, six Jews, four Germans, one Pole and one Norwegian, with one not determined. The museum says the Nazi occupiers used the killings for anti-Semitic propaganda, and that after 1944 the Soviet authorities did not allow the victims to be commemorated. It describes the killings as having become "a neutral statistic" until a 2016 exhibition in the former KGB headquarters in Riga.

Dubno, in Rivne oblast, shows how the evidence has come back to light. Euromaidan Press, reporting on an excavation by the Dolia Search and Memorial Centre in 2019, cites a German military police report of 1 July 1941. The report, drawn up by the 48th Panzer Corps, says the NKVD had executed 400 ethnic Germans and Ukrainians in Dubno prison. Local residents told German troops, who reached the town on 26 June, that about 400 political prisoners had been executed on the orders of an NKVD commissioner. When German soldiers entered the prison on 27 June, they found relatives searching the bodies.

The centre dug pits in the prison yard in 2019 and found 19 bodies, including three women. Four had been shot in the head. Anthropologist Olha Minenko, of the Institute of Archaeology of the National Academy of Sciences, said the bodies had been buried with their arms folded and knees bent, which suggested burial about three days after death. The Euromaidan article also says that the number and nationality of the Dubno dead remain unknown, and that the victims were Ukrainians and ethnic Germans according to documents and testimony. The local mayor said the topic had been taboo and that the city had filed a criminal complaint so that forensic examinations could take place.

The sources do not agree, and the differences are substantial. The National WWII Museum's range for western Ukraine is 10,000 to 40,000. The Euromaidan Press, citing the archive, gives 24 thousand for western Ukraine. For Lviv, the Soviet archive figure cited by the Kyiv Post is 1,366, the museum's own figure is about 1,700, and the posters Himka cites give three separate figures for the three prisons, and these are not added together here. For Dubno the German report gives 400, while the excavation of 2019 found 19 bodies in a deep pit, and its organisers said the total was still unknown. The Rainiai figure is 73 on one page of the heritage site and 75 on another.

These gaps reflect how the records were made. Some lists are original NKVD documents with resolutions signed by officers, such as one from Lviv prison number four that carries the resolution "I authorize the execution of the enemies of the nation". Other lists were compiled in the 1990s from exhumations, archival work and witness statements. The Electronic Archive of the Ukrainian liberation movement, a joint project of a Lviv research centre, Lviv University and the Lontsky Street museum, held 23,543 documents when the Euromaidan Press reported on it in 2016. Its collection includes memoirs of prisoners who survived, such as Bohdan Kazanivskyi, who described muffled shots from the basement of a Lviv prison and then a sudden silence on the night of 23 to 24 June.

The Euromaidan Press also reports that Beria gave official permission for the executions on 4 July 1941, even though the killings had begun in June. It says the German advance was so rapid that the prison staff did not have time to prepare enough railway wagons to evacuate the prisoners, so the NKVD chose to kill those who could not be moved. The article describes two train cars of prisoners thrown off a bridge into the precipice formed by the Dniester river at Zalischyky. It also says that most of the guilt of those executed was never proven.

The killings were largely hidden for decades. The Understanding Society article notes that the prison massacres were not well documented until the past decade, and that Soviet and later Russian secrecy about the NKVD made the events hard to study. The 2017 sourcebook edited by Kiebuzinski and Motyl, which the article describes as mainly a collection of documents, was intended to let other scholars investigate the details. Its editors describe the killings as the work of Soviet authorities and say that the victims were visible in the towns the Red Army left behind.

Memorials are contested too. The Lontsky Street prison museum was founded in 2009 after citizens' campaigns demanded it, and was made a national museum that October. The Kyiv Post reported in 2010 that the government had not allocated money for the museum that year, and that its future was uncertain. In Dubno, the council planned a memorial at the site, which the mayor described as a cemetery.

What is still unclear is the total. The surviving records are uneven, and the excavations described here cover only some of the sites. The accounts from Lutsk, Lviv, Dubno, Telšiai, Riga and the other towns agree on the broad method, and most of the victims were political prisoners or men held without trial. They differ on how many died in each town, and it is on those figures that the historians still argue.
